result.summary: Pausanias explains how Achaia, once Ægialus, got its names. Xuthus and his son Ion came to Ægialus, Ion married Helice and the people became Ionians, and later the Achæans, driven from Argos and Lacedæmon by the Dorians, defeated the Ionians, who then migrated to Attica.

scenes.title: Names of Achaia
scenes.summary: Pausanias explains the old name Ægialus and the modern name Achaia.

scenes.title: Xuthus, Ion and Helice
scenes.summary: Xuthus is exiled, goes to Athens and then Ægialus. His son Ion marries Helice, inherits the kingdom and renames the people Ionians; he dies in Attica.
scenes.stakes: Xuthus and Ion risk exile and war, and Ion risks losing a kingdom he is trying to win.

scenes.title: Why Argives were called Achæans
scenes.summary: The sons of Achæus settled in Argos, married daughters of Danaus, and their power spread the name Achæan.

scenes.title: Achæans fight Ionians
scenes.summary: Expelled by the Dorians, the Achæans under Tisamenus propose union; the Ionians refuse, Tisamenus dies, and the Achæans win. The Ionians later settle in Attica under Melanthus.
scenes.stakes: Tisamenus and the Ionians risk losing their lives, kingship and homeland.

alias_notes.explanation: The Argives were privately called Danai, after Danaus.
The old name of the country.

notable_quotes.reason: Homer's line preserves the ancient name of the region.

analysis.text: The chapter explains place names and peoples through migrations and genealogy, tying Achaia to Athens, Thessaly and Argos.
It reflects the Greek tradition of the Dorian return displacing Achæans and the Ionian migration to Asia Minor via Attica.

fun_facts.text: The Homeric line quoted is from the Catalogue of Ships in the Iliad.

language_notes.text: Ægialus likely derives from the Greek for sea-shore (aigialos), which is why some explain the name by the country's coastal position.
"Decide which of his sons should be king" means Xuthus acted as arbitrator among the sons of Erechtheus over the succession.
A quotation from Homer's Iliad, Book 2, the Catalogue of Ships, listing the contingents under Agamemnon.
Metanastes is Greek for one who has moved elsewhere, an immigrant, so the name shows the family's foreign origin in Argos.
Danai refers to the people of Danaus, an earlier king of Argos; Homer also uses Danaans for the Greeks generally.
Phiditia was the Spartan public mess, where citizens took common meals.

context_notes.text: Erechtheus was a legendary king of Athens, so Xuthus's marriage gave his sons Athenian royal connections.
The Dorians' invasion of the Peloponnese, called the Return of the Heracleidae, displaced the Achæans in Greek tradition.
Tisamenus was the son of Orestes, the famous son of Agamemnon, which explains his prestige as a king of ancient lineage.
Melanthus was a king of Athens who, in tradition, came from Messenia and took the throne after the Dorian invasion.

literary_notes.text: The Ionian leaders are shown as fearful and jealous, rejecting union for political reasons, which contrasts with Tisamenus's bravery and renown.
The Athenians' welcome looks like gratitude, but the alternative tradition suggests it was really fear, which undercuts the generous motive.
